summary:
Arkhangelsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The sources assembled for this record contain no oblast-specific finding, so the assessment describes the conditions a visitor to Arkhangelsk faces on arrival under federal law.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (June 2025) states that same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no legislation covering sexual orientation or gender identity protects people in housing, healthcare or employment. A trans visitor has no legal route to recognised documents, no access to gender-affirming care, and no discrimination remedy.

Public expression is itself an offence. 'Gay propaganda' charges carry fines of up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and a repeat offence can be prosecuted criminally with up to four years in prison. The Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, in force from January 2024, makes participation punishable by two to six years' imprisonment and organising by six to ten years.

The volume of enforcement is documented. The Home Office note records at least 139 people affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between December 2022 and March 2024. Human Rights Watch counted 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the designation as of 30 June 2025, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. Across 98 court cases covering 81 people, judges convicted for displaying banned symbols. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years.

The Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates, and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia, regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and its advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation.
tangentialFactors:
Liability attaches to expression and to association rather than to conduct alone. Human Rights Watch's administrative convictions rest on displaying alleged symbols, and the May 2025 charges against publishing-house staff rest on the sale of fiction; a visitor can be swept into the regime through a book purchase, clothing, or a social-media post rather than through any act directed at another person.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million roubles into the state budget in the preceding two years.

Coercive practice against transgender people extends beyond the courts. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 on a transgender woman lured by relatives in 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. An Associated Press report of December 2024 recorded a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The US advisory applies to every traveller regardless of identity, so the risk assessment does not turn on whether a visitor is visibly transgender; arbitrary law enforcement and wrongful detention are cited as general hazards. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia, a recommendation that bears on onward planning rather than on entry.
localsOnly:
Residents convicted of displaying banned LGBT+ symbols face administrative fines of up to 2,000 roubles, and a repeat display is punishable under the criminal code by up to four years in prison. The extremist designation carries two to six years for participation and six to ten years for organising.

No national legislation covering sexual orientation or gender identity provides protection in housing, healthcare or employment, so residents who are dismissed, refused treatment or evicted have no statutory claim. Legal gender transition is banned outright and trans-specific healthcare was effectively ended in 2023, which removes document correction and medical access for residents as well as visitors.

Residents who leave the country may find the protection machinery aligned with them: the Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims, and the note assesses trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
No oblast-specific finding appears in the sources for this record. There is no documented count of prosecutions, raids, detentions or administrative fines recorded in Arkhangelsk Oblast, and no sourced description of local police or court practice in the oblast as distinct from the national pattern.

Implementation of the 2023 federal ban on trans-specific healthcare by clinics in Arkhangelsk is not sourced. Whether oblast institutions continued to prescribe, or refused existing patients, is unresolved here.

The travel advisories cited do not describe conditions at Arkhangelsk airport, at border crossing points, or in the oblast's detention facilities; their warnings are national in scope. The oblast's distance from the North Caucasus, the one region the Home Office singles out, is not itself addressed by any source, and no finding establishes a differing risk level for northern Russia.
